text: About 16,000 years ago, the Jōmon people lived on the islands of Japan.
They hunted deer and wild boar, fished, and gathered nuts and acorns from the forests.
src: The Jōmon culture flourished in the Japanese archipelago from about 14,000 to 300 BCE
People also ate sika deer, wild boar, freshwater fish and wild plants / Beeches, buckeyes, chestnuts and oaks gave nuts and acorns

text: Jōmon potters made the oldest known pottery in the world, pressing cords into the wet clay to make patterns.
They also made lacquered wooden objects, and they looked after groves of lacquer and chestnut trees.
src: Jōmon potters made the world’s oldest known ceramics / The typical decoration was made by pressing cords into the wet clay
lacquered wooden objects / There is evidence that they tended groves of chestnut and lacquer trees

text: The Jōmon left no writing, so we learn about their beliefs from the things they made.
Curved stone beads called magatama were placed in graves with the dead.
src: The Jōmon left no writing, so their beliefs can only be inferred from what they made and how they treated their dead
magatama, curved stone beads, changed from a common ornament found in homes into grave goods placed with the dead

text: About 2,900 years ago, villages like those in Korea appeared in Japan, with rice farming and bronze and iron.
For a long time these villages stood alongside the villages of the Jōmon.
src: from around 900 BCE Korean-type settlements were founded in western Kyushu. Their settlers brought wet rice farming, bronze and iron metallurgy
their villages seem to have existed alongside those of the Jōmon and Yayoi for around a thousand years

text: The Jōmon mixed with rice farmers, and people in Japan today carry part of their ancestry.
In the far north, on Hokkaido, two Jōmon groups joined to become the ancestors of the Ainu.
src: The Jōmon people mixed with the Yayoi, and modern Japanese carry part of their ancestry
In Hokkaido, two distinct Jōmon populations later merged to form the proto-Ainu
